summary: We developed the Earth–Moon Analog Explorer, an interactive web platform that identifies, compares, and evaluates terrestrial geological structures—such as impact craters and volcanic formations—against their lunar and Martian counterparts.   Our project addresses the challenge of assessing the feasibility and probability of discovering terrestrial analog zones for pre-mission testing. By cross-referencing custom geological research with institutional catalogs (the IAU/USGS Gazetteer and the Earth Impact Database), the platform pairs over 35 Earth sites with specific lunar features, including Artemis III candidate landing regions at the lunar south pole. Each site is mapped to operational testing objectives—such as rover traction on steep slopes, ground-penetrating radar, subsurface drilling, and astronaut EVA training—while tracing every metric to its primary source.   This tool is vital because establishing permanent lunar bases and future Martian stations requires rigorous Earth-based validation. By pinpointing the most probable and accurate proving grounds on Earth, the platform helps mission planners de-risk hardware, test life-support and navigation systems, and bridge planetary geology with real-world space station engineering.
details:
Earth–Moon Analog Explorer is an interactive research platform built to evaluate terrestrial impact craters and volcanic structures as proving grounds for future lunar and Martian missions. Before building permanent stations on the Moon, space agencies need reliable places on Earth to test rovers, habitats, and excavation tools under realistic geological conditions. Our project focuses on assessing the feasibility and probability of identifying and utilizing these analog zones so mission planners can match specific lunar engineering challenges with the right terrestrial environments.

The platform works by combining our own research database of over 35 terrestrial sites across all seven continents with official planetary catalogs, specifically the IAU/USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature and the Earth Impact Database (PASSC/UNB). Each terrestrial site is paired with its closest lunar counterpart—ranging from equatorial craters and basaltic maria to high-priority Artemis III candidate landing regions at the lunar south pole, such as Shackleton, Cabeus, Haworth, and de Gerlache. Rather than just comparing visual appearance, the system maps each location to concrete operational testing objectives. For example, users can filter sites suited for testing rover wheel traction on slopes steeper than 20 degrees (such as Tabun-Khara-Obo in Mongolia or Wolfe Creek in Australia), calibrating LiDAR and spectrometers, running ground-penetrating radar (GPR) over buried or subglacial structures (like Hiawatha in Greenland or Kalkkop in South Africa), or training astronauts in subsurface drilling and geological sampling (such as Nördlinger Ries in Germany).

A core benefit of the tool is its strict data provenance. When compiling geological data from multiple sources, we frequently encountered missing coordinates, age estimates expressed as broad geological epochs instead of numeric values, and geometric discrepancies. Rather than hiding these gaps, we built an automated verification and flagging system into the platform. Every record clearly states whether its data comes from a verified institutional catalog, peer-reviewed mission literature (such as LRO LOLA, Diviner, and LCROSS data), or unverified student research, while automatically flagging anomalies like inconsistent area-to-diameter ratios. This transparency ensures that engineers and researchers know the exact reliability of the data they are working with.

To build the application, we used React 18, TypeScript/JavaScript, and HTML5/CSS3 for the interactive user interface, alongside Lucide React for iconography. On the data layer, we implemented Zod to enforce strict runtime schema validation across all geological records, ensuring that coordinates, dimensions, and source citations remain consistent. We structured our initial dataset in Google Sheets and cross-referenced chronostratigraphic ages using International Commission on Stratigraphy (ICS) boundaries.

Our approach stands out because it treats analog site selection as an operational engineering tool rather than a static encyclopedia. We also made a deliberate effort to look beyond traditional northern-hemisphere training sites by integrating lesser-known, high-potential locations in the Southern Hemisphere—including Argentine sites like Campo del Cielo, Bajada del Diablo, Río Cuarto, and Barda Negra, as well as Monturaqui in Chile. Throughout development, our team balanced morphological similarity (simple bowl craters versus complex multi-ring basins), surface composition, and testing utility, while also accounting for environmental factors that Earth cannot naturally replicate, such as hard vacuum, anhydrous abrasive regolith, and the extreme cryogenic temperatures of lunar polar cold traps. Ultimately, the intended impact of our project is to make pre-mission planning more accessible, data-driven, and globally inclusive, helping reduce technical risks on Earth before deploying hardware and crews to real stations on the Moon.
